newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin pre-operative tests to last extra two days.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin pre-operative tests to last extra two days.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is to spend two more days in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital for more tests ahead of his planned heart surgery, the Kremlin press office said on Monday.

As doctors consider when best to perform the bypass operation to relieve the 65-year-old president's clogged cardiac arteries, Russian officials and the world at large have been left guessing who will control the nuclear superpower during the operation.
Yeltsin went into hospital on Friday for a series of medical checks which, his aides say, are routine before such operations.
Spokesmen initially said he would spend the weekend in the clinic, where his wife Naina is currently convalescing after a kidney operation last month.

On Monday, the Kremlin announced that Yeltsin would spend two more days as an in-patient. But it gave no details of what tests would be carried out -- nor would it say whether the apparent extension of the president's stay was unforeseen.

Yeltsin broke a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of Moscow's leaders earlier this month when he said he was going to have an operation on his heart. The alternative, the president said on television, was a sedentary life.

Yeltsin, who had two heart attacks last year, disappeared between the two rounds of this year's presidential election, prompting speculation he had been taken ill. He left for a holiday outside Moscow a fortnight ago.
He agreed earlier this month to have a heart bypass to improve blood supply to the heart and doctors will decide later this month exactly when to operate.

Bypass surgery is much more common in the United States and other Western countries than in Russia. The Kremlin has invited experienced Western cardiologists to join the team of consultants deciding how best to treat the president.
Yeltsin has said he will have the operation in Russia rather than travelling abroad for treatment.
His absence has prompted speculation about who would take the reins when the president had his operation and who would hold the "red button" triggering Russia's nuclear arsenal.
On Sunday, NTV commercial television said Yeltsin may hand over the "nuclear button" to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin only for as long as he is unconscious during surgery.

"We have learnt from Kremlin sources that just before the the operation starts the president will sign a decree handing over the "nuclear button' to Viktor Chernomyrdin for a very short period of time," NTV said.
"Immediately after the operation, when the doctors take the president out of the anaesthetic, he will sign a new decree taking back control..." it added.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said last week that Yeltsin was considering different options but gave no clue as to what the final option could be.

Under the constitution, the prime minister takes over as caretaker ahead of new elections if the president is permanently incapacitated. But the 1993 basic law makes no mention of a temporary handover of power.
